summary:
Earthrise is an interactive web platform designed to make it easier and faster to evaluate and choose landing sites at the Moon’s south pole. Because this area has many potential resources, the platform connects the goals of NASA’s Artemis program with a simple interface that anyone can use. Planning missions in this region is very difficult because of the extreme terrain, permanently shadowed regions (PSR), and changing angles. These factors make it hard to balance sunlight for energy, safe ground for landing, and direct communication with Earth (DTE) at the same time.
To improve on existing tools that are too complex and separate, Earthrise analyzes space data, digital elevation models (DEM), and custom coordinates. It then gives a fast evaluation using a traffic-light system and 2D and 3D visuals. Its flexible design is divided into three levels:
1. A public mode with simple visual indicators and easy-to-understand graphics.
2. An educational level with elevation and power data for students.
3. An expert mode with crater comparison tables, terrain editors, and advanced energy calculations for planners and engineers.
In this way, Earthrise makes scientific information accessible to everyone and serves as a fast, educational tool with a big impact.
details:
Earthrise is an innovative interactive web platform designed to evaluate and choose landing sites, mainly at the Moon’s south pole. It connects NASA’s Artemis missions with an interface that is easy for everyone to use. It solves the challenge of planning in a region with extreme terrain, permanently shadowed areas, and difficult conditions for energy and direct communication with Earth.

By analyzing surface and space data, it provides a quick evaluation using traffic-light status indicators and 2D and 3D graphics. It has three adapted levels:

  • A public mode with simple indicators.
  • An educational level for students.
  • An expert mode with crater tables and advanced energy calculations.

The platform was built mainly using HTML and interactive web technologies, with help from artificial intelligence tools to improve and organize the code. For its ideas and data, it uses records from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO), LOLA elevation data, and space tracking data from JPL (Horizons), along with specialized books on engineering and thermodynamics.

Our creative approach solves a very technical and scattered problem—measuring the angles and energy of the lunar poles—through a flexible interface. It changes the difficulty of the data depending on the user's skill level (general public, educator, or expert), combining interactive 3D graphics with a fast, traffic-light visual check that did not exist in such a complete way before. We carefully considered the physical and environmental conditions of the lunar south pole, major past missions, and the latest lunar orbit completed by the Artemis II crew.
